Rezzett’s 3rd album ‘Into the Boiling Darks’ is now presented as 21 individual tracks, scraping their bin juice-soaked barrel for grittiest morsels of mutant dance music, now primed for DJ use, and also as a proper 72 minute dunk in their bilgy sound. You probably know what to expect from their 13 years of crooked productions, both in duo and solo as Tapes & Lukid, and it doesn’t disappoint for levels of thee scuzziest, sawn-off dance noise blatz.

They’ve clearly reserved some of the dankest in the dungeon for this album, laying it down thick and fuming in a mix of mildewed ambient vignettes, blown-out beatdown, Actress-alike deep bleep trodders, hobbled proto-house and fizzy clangerz that know no chill. If pushed to play faves, the Skaters-esque horn of ‘Bliss Up’ is one, as is the faded, romantic jungle tekno lustre of ‘Kissing Twelve’ and ‘Bongo Tax’, thru the manic rush of ‘In The Loneleyz’ and ‘Nirvana’, or the teeth-chatter gnash of ‘Kopli’, but it’s simply all gravy.

Planted and watered by Horn of Plenty's Deutsche operative Nein Rodere (aka David Roeder) and Providence-based PPM-affiliated Nowhere Flower (aka Lila Jarzombek), Nein Flower roots itself in wyrd folk and outsider musick history, sucking up nutrients from Christina Carter, Sun City Girls, The Shadow Ring and Jandek in the process.

We can't be sure whether Roeder and Jarzombek were in the same room together when these ramshackle tracks were made, but 'Nein Flower' sounds spontaneous in a way that feels unconnected to modern wireless technology. They're both visual artists as well as musicians, and found a deep connection, despite growing up on different continents. And although both locations clearly feed into the music - Berlin's restless, punkish isolation and Providence's basement-dwelling, lo-fidelity introspection - the session sounds like it was recorded from beginning to end in a third space, directly to tape. 

It's as if Graham Lambkin and Darren Harris (circa 'City Lights') were tasked with recording an early Charalambides side - blown out, dissonant and poetic - but strangely tuned in with folk history, too. Both Roeder and Jarzombek seem to share all duties, with Jarzombek's smudgy coos wisping and whirling around Roeder's surreal Lou Reed-inspired narrations and instrumentation, appearing and falling away unceremoniously. 

Nein Flower is about capturing the moment; an impromptu back-and-forth that’s fully mesmerising. In the accompanying press release, the duo talk about naïve art and no-frills performance; composition, they explain, is landscape painting and their details are fully revealed when you look a little closer, finding elements that are less obviously premeditated. And honestly, it's a technique that works for them - not only does the album feel completely honest in a way that's genuinely charming, but it places them in an unusual artistic plane that's teetering between nostalgia and innovation. It's tangible, messy and alluring stuff, intimate, often grotesque, always compelling.

5 Gate Temple’s Danish binds yield another crooked gem with sound artist Victoria Mingot’s enchantingly casual, even barely-there, lower case strums and murmurs, like diaries of broken sleep FFO Joane Robertson, Loren Connors, Graham Lambkin.

5GT’s Danish affiliations now reach to Victoria Mingot and ‘God Spill’, which takes CPH’s lonely solo songwriter thing to its quietest, most ruminative depths. Her dozen pieces are mostly instrumental, defined by plaintive melodic structuring for acoustic guitar on what sounds like dictaphone recordings that imbue everything with a eerie intimacy. However, there are vocals, and they’re pretty special when they do appear, like a flickering filament in the aether of ‘i saw the sign’, recalling Mary Maddox off Mike Ratledge’s ‘Riddles of the Sphinx’, floating, Virginia Astley-like, on the frayed Lambkin-esque strum of ‘in plentitude of the harvest’, or more textural in the mournful raga meditation ‘om dhyana’.

This exquisitely discreet balance of unshowy yet transfixing instrumental economy makes other works such as ‘before you fly’ stand out even more for its shimmering blend of Joanne Robertson and Loren Connors-like substance, and the whole record fully reveals itself with repeat listens.

items.body:
Chicago cohorts Natural Information Society and Bitchin' Bajas present their two collaborative albums as a single 2CD package.

Released 10 years before 'Totality', 'Autoimaginary' introduced Bitchin Bajas and Natural Information Society's ongoing collaboration with a cosmic wave of drone and spiritual jazz energy.  While not quite as time-disintegrating as it follow-up, it provides a tantalizing first taste of their collaboration. It's the first side, the 20-minute 'On No Fade' where 'Automaginary' really blossoms. Without getting bogged down in jazz and funk logic, working on a wide-open canvas with billowing drones that swirl around the frame, smudging into washy percussion that never properly materializes, the group of players sound as if they're having a blast, almost lifting themselves into the heavens before the track fades to silence.

And although the flip, that's split into four shorter segments, is still enjoyable, anchored by motorik grooves ('Anemometer'), Dorothy Ashby-style devotional harp runs ('Tricks Me Mind') and furious rhythms from Abrams and drummers Frank Rosaly and Mikel Avery, it takes until the title track for the band to regain their sense of awe. 

Splitting their sophomore collab into disorientated side-long contemplations of "space" and "time", they  puzzle out the divine symmetry between spiritual jazz and polychromatic new age gear. They've refined their cooperation here, choosing to separate their dronier, more new age compositions on the first ("space") side, and the deliberate, transcendent free jazz jams on the flip ("time", natch). 

The extended title track is up first, and it's flawlessly blurry, losing Abrahams' signature guimbri plucks in crystalline synth and woodwind gesticulations that freeze and liquify until Mikel Patrick Avery's soft focus rhythms draw all the sounds together in the final act. And although 'Nothing Does Not Show' is comparatively brief, it offers a more structured counterpart, scratching at the same theme but fading Abrahams' lithe double bass and Lisa Alvarado's harmonium quivers into the foreground alongside Crain's tremolo organ and Rob Frye's swirling flutes.

And although the balance is markedly different on Side B's 'Always 9 Seconds Away', it's equally as crushing. Dilating the tempo to a crawling, Bohren-like 40bpm, Avery just glances the drum heads, opening up time (and space, tbh) for Frye and bass clarinetist Jason Stein to haunt the emptiness with a permed woodwind duet. The sound's topped off with eerily ornate organ and synth vamps, and the result is like a half-speed Don Cherry, dazed from stretched tape and temporal disintegration. It's so good that the jammy, full-throttle finale 'Clock no Clock' kinda pales in comparison, but that's a minor grievance; if you're gonna study time, it should probably go both ways, right?

items.body:
Deaf Center member Otto A Totland’s 2014 debut LP, an intricate work for solo piano.

"Otto A Totland's modern compositional elements are most widely recognized as half of the Norwegian duo Deaf Center, where his melancholic, intricate piano work provides haunting relief to the beds of noise and deep strings from Erik K Skodvin. Pinô is the first full-length release by Totland, though his solo work has been released once, as the 5-minute A-side of Sonic Pieces 7inch Harmony From the Past. Otto's previously brief vignettes are now expanded into a fully personal realization of his own style.

Initial track Open fills itself with heavy, knowing pauses that quickly become overwhelmed with the desire to understand what's to come. Each silence leads into quick flutters of keys, preparing the listener for a vast terrain of giddy beauty, bleak depths, and true contentedness. Pinô quickly recalls deep winter; in front of a fireplace for days on end, you lose how far along you've ventured into the 18 tracks without any idea how far is left to go. The experience feels inevitable, with no other option but to curl up somewhere cozy and appreciate the sense of timelessness that Totland has created. His album is a haunting modern compositional treasure, expressed through instrumentals completely unique to Totland and captured masterfully by Nils Frahm at Durton Studios.

With Pinô, Otto A Totland appears out of the Norwegian landscape, sharing an achievement that will provide a relief during the brooding winter darkness. Though a highly personal endeavor, the recognizable continuation of Totland’s compositions will attract fans of Deaf Center, and the cinematic and classical components of his solo work will hold sway for those familiar with Harold Budd or Dustin O’Halloran."

Picked up by Ninja Tune after a highly acclaimed release on Smalltown Supersound in 2002, this excellent outfit featured members from the Norwegian jazz, improv and electronics scene to make up what was akin to a Charles Mingus big band for the 23rd century.

"Early this year remarkable reviews began to appear in the British music press for the latest sensations to come out of Scandinavia. There was a difference to many of the other acts earning Norway its reputation at the time, though. Jaga Jazzist is what can only be described as a supergroup. The ten members of the band are also active participants in, Kim Hiorthoy's group, Bobby Hughes Experience, Bugges Wesseltoft, Motorpsycho, Big Bang, Euroboys, Jazzkammer, Biosphere, Supersilent, Alog and Lasse Marhaug, covering every type of music from electronica, nu-jazz and rock. Jaga Jazzist are well known in Norway for contributing to almost every quality Norwegian record released in recent times.

The comparisons reached for by the press were as broad as they get - from Talk Talk, Soft Machine, Eric Satie, John Coltrane and Don Cherry to acts like Aphex Twin, Stereolab, Squarepusher, Isotope 217 and Tortoise. This range sums up the breadth and originality of the group's sound. Jaga Jazzist are indeed a musical one off who’s arsenal includes trumpets, trombone, electric guitar, bass, tuba, two bass clarinets, Fender Rhodes and vibraphone, and it is the mixture of these instruments with a sometimes harsh electronic edge that really makes the music stand out. It is melodic, delicate and subtle but a million miles from wallpaper music. It is music that demands and rewards attention, further proof that you don't have to shout to avoid being lazy chill-out-by-numbers.

The group came to the attention of Ninja Tune who will be releasing their work outside of Norway from now on and while "A Livingroom Hush" garnered critical acclaim , its distribution was patchy. Hence, this re-release, complete with the very odd but very wonderful Monty-Python-on-safari promo video from "Animal Chin".

It's a journey into sounds and moods that manages to sound both classic and contemporary and is an oasis to anyone interested in music which combines iconoclasm with beauty, melody with avant gardism and, in general, a complete lack of interest in anything other than good music."

items.body:
In spring 2025, Abul Mogard and Rafael Anton Irisarri created the source material for their second album, Where Light Pauses in the Silence of the Sun, during a three-day residency at Morphine Raum in Berlin.

"Functioning as both recording studio and performance venue, the space has no stage, with the audience gathered around the performers. Working within an open framework, the duo reshaped the music each evening while recording the performances live to multitrack. Rotary speakers, modular synthesizers and bowed guitar formed the core of their sonic language, captured through a 1970s mixing console and microphones placed around the room.

Back in Mogard’s studio in Rome, the material was further crafted as motifs were stretched, fragments isolated, and tempos dissolved. Irisarri recorded additional guitar textures and treatments in New York, while passages recorded by Martina Bertoni and Andrea Burelli in Berlin reinforced the harmonic centres and brought breath, refinement and a new sensibility to their compositions. The process continued as Mogard’s layering and subtraction reassembled everyone’s parts into the final arrangement.

The album opens with “In the Eastern Wild,” building from a sparse outline into a monumental formation of low-frequency weight, its internal motion shaped by the rotating Leslie speaker. “Over the Domes” widens into a broader acoustic field, where sustained modular tones meet waves of softly plucked guitar. The music then turns inward with “A Blue Descent,” centred on Bertoni’s cello, whose growling timbre introduces a melancholic depth.

At the album’s centre, “In a Quiet Radiance” unfolds around a slow guitar ostinato, its luminous stillness opening into a more expansive and reflective state. Across its ten-minute span, Burelli’s violin lines and Bertoni’s lower cello phrases gradually surface, weaving through the harmonic field. Mogard brings Burelli’s processed voice to the fore, its emotive, operatic presence becoming one of the record’s pivotal moments. “Of Blessed Ages” suspends the sonic flow, shifting between parallel major and minor chords as lingering, slowly decaying melodies shape the music’s internal drift. The closing “Among Shadows” settles into a darker resonance as layered textures recede.

Mogard and Irisarri’s shared language balances restraint and maximalism. UK magazine Crack describes the music as “a tidal wave held in suspension,” while Dutch newspaper de Volkskrant writes, “What a colossal sound, and how this music strikes at the emotions.” Reflecting on the residency sessions, Irisarri recalls: “At moments I genuinely couldn’t tell if a sound was coming from me or from Abul. It stopped feeling like two people making decisions and began to feel like we were inside a system moving on its own."

Marja de Sanctis’ cover artwork revisits the vessel sculpture from the duo’s first album, Impossibly Distant, Impossibly Close. There it appeared as raw, unfired clay. Here it has been fired in the kiln and finished with a glaze. Light gathers on its polished surface and spills into the surrounding space. As she explains, “I wanted to convey the idea of continuity within the duo, and the vessel became a kind of container for that idea. However, their music felt different this time, and with the collaboration of Martina and Andrea, I felt it should have a sleeker, softer, more glamorous look, very distant from the first raw appearance.” The transformation of the vessel from raw clay to fired form suggests a passage from immediacy toward permanence, mirroring the music’s gradual expansion."

Vibrant reminders of the Éthiopiques series’ peerless ‘60s/‘70s brilliance, collated by Francis Falcetto, the man who brought the sounds back into circulation via Buda Musique in the late ‘90s.

First introduced to us by Shackleton, and maybe best known to many for heavy rotation on Jim Jarmusch’s ‘Broken Flowers’ (2005), the Éthiopiques series showcases a relatively short-lived but incredible explosion of jazz, funk and Afrobeat-adjacent grooves that emerged from Addis Ababa in the ‘60s, mostly issued on the labels Amha, Kaifa, and Philips-Ethiopia, but sadly all curtailed by political revolution by the late ‘70s. 

For the uninitiated or keen admirers ‘Heavenly Ethiopiques: The Best Of The Ethiopiques Series’ yields a best-of cornucopia of infectious tunes by the sound’s founding fathers - Mulatu Astatke, Mahmoud Ahmed and Tilahun Gessesse - and their crackshot players, such as Wallias Band, sequencing a range of blazing to cool, and always sophisticated, vocal tunes and taut, breakbeat-led instrumentals bound to ignite love for this sound or rekindle old passions.

items.body:
LA musician Aaron MF Olson debuts on Country Thyme Records - his second ‘songs for singing’ album in just over a decade of releasing music.

"Aaron’s a sweet fellow. He can be salty on occasion, but it’s put to good use here. His songs mix satiric, confessional and experimental lyric modes and his music’s cut from a fine cloth of head-in- formed, classically sweet and soft pop/rock modes. Most of all, Songs Album II is music for listening.

To listen to and to play music; that's been his highest aim, for most of his life. His high school band was a post-rock group that morphed into a surf music outfit; he’s been similarly guided by such polarities ‘n congruities in the time since. He’s released four albums of “Baywatch Krautrock” with LA Takedown, and played and recorded in many other projects, including but not limited to his experimental Music Tracing Ensemble, exotica collective Other Delights, Bedouine, Coffin Prick, Papa M, Tommy Peltier, Vetiver and “L.A.’s Most grateful Dead cover band,” Richard Pictures. Aaron’s solo credits include 2020’s switched-on essay, Ranchera '22 {Synthesizer Interpretations of the Songs of José Alfredo Jiménez} and the 2022 New Age release, For Dorothy. He does film/television composition too; most recently, the Original Motion Picture Soundtrack for Matt Hewitt’s indie horror film, Hoagie. Life’s not cheap, and so far as hard work goes, making music is fun.

If all this implies a wide palette of input/output, Songs Album II has it in reserve, framed scrupulously in a sequence of nice, light folk/rock ditties, their spacey-yet-precise arrangements colorfully blowing up the songs’ personal values: by definition, perfect listening! It’s Aaron, on most acoustic and electric guitars and basses, keyboards, harmonica, synth & vocals, Robin MacMillian on drums, Tara Milch, flute; Michael Sachs, clarinets; Luke Csehak, bassoon & trumpet; additional guitars & vocals from Blue Broderick, Bart Davenport and Wayne Faler; keyboards & vocals from Andrew Dorsett and vocals by Matt Popieluch, making Songs Album II a collection of widescreen, hi-def songs and sounds.

Aaron’s voice is light-toned, gentle and tunefully raspy, falling somewhere between Jack Nitzsche, Van Dyke Parks, Robert Wyatt, and personal inspirations John Simon, Stephen Pastel, Jim O’Rourke and Kermit’s nephew, Robin. And Emmett Otter! Not a bad bunch to be sharing the water with. He came late to singing; 2021’s Songs Album was literally provoked into being. He’d was down with COVID, a lifeless, cold week, sweating it out… and immediately afterwards, he finished several already-conceived songs, wrote the rest, got it all done in weeks — a post-fever fervor! Without trying to, Aaron came around to Songs Album II in the EXACT same way, after another bout of demon COVID. He’s a singer/songwriter who’s been known to dream musical passages, with a couple on this record in delightful proof — welcoming the hand of the mystic upon him.

The “no particular theme” implied by the title is only part so. It’s no concept album, unless the concept is “album, of songs,” but there ARE themes to be found here, feels and emotions crystalized around this lifetime of listening. With moments of sound laced into song, functioning both as toe-tapping sweet melodies and near-Joycean full-function index of personal reference, Aaron MF Olson’s Songs Album II is music meant for listening to in the spirit of listening, and higher calling. And singing along!"

Pensive to strangely sublime electroacoustic abstraction and frisson from cellist-composer/sound designer Martina Bertoni & TAL’s bossman and To Rococo Rot / Mapstation legend) Stefan Schneider, quietly undergoing each other in their intuitive process.

‘Holding on and letting go’ manifests the duo’s mutual fascination for musical economy in restricted electronic palettes that unfold as a pair of time-slipping works defined by incremental metamorphosis. They land in the label’s 10th year of operations after that ace Garth Erasmus LP to continue an ever-roving, dot-joining agenda at its most oblique yet subtly absorbing.

In ‘Holding On’ they almost subliminally transition from folk drone wheeze to iridescent ambient noise with a spellbinding semi-organic quality, where the smallest gestures become amplified in butterfly effect chain reaction of microcosmic clinamen, producing low key entrancing results. 

On ‘Letting Go’ Bertoni’s cello is more discernible, yet likewise melts into air with alluring nuance, fraying and congealing into a sort of plasmic jazz x ambient noise abstract, calling to mind the queasy air movements of Joachim Nordwall pieces or CMvH’s paranormal studies gone more exotic, humid.

Featuring MØ, Quiet Light, Koilwood, Helena Gao and others, Copenhagen duo A Good Year's second album is another slick set of trip-hop inspired Danish pop from the reliable Escho stable, home of Smerz, Astrid Sonne, Iceage and Snuggle.

Albert Hildebrand and Tobias Laust Hansen didn't have a fixed idea in mind when they started work on 'Play'. As the title suggests, it emerged from just playing, improvising with each other and shuttling recordings back and forth between their collaborators. "The music became a vessel for connection," they explain. "A way to reach to people we admire, but also a way to create a social element within these sometimes introverted jams." And their approach leads to an uncommonly light set of almost-pop; it's still as neatly polished as anything from the fertile Copenhagen scene, but there's a willing naivety that allows breathing room, a way for errors to slip in and humanize the material in the face of AI perfection.

Fine collaborator Koilwood shows up on the charming 'Back of a car', whispering softly over Hildebrand and Hansen's skipping lo-fi beats and skeletal instrumentation and Tiffi Malmgren lends her voice to early highlight 'Flight', a slo-mo trip-hop dream that's lifted by the duo's tape-warped piano vamps and hazy textures. And Malmgren returns with Major Lazer collaborator MØ (yep it was her on 'Lean On') on the album's stand-out 'Blue Flame', an electrified indie anthem that makes good use of the Danish singers' unique, recognizable voices. Scandi pop lovers, this'll hit the spot.

Arvo Pärt has become something of a yardstick by which contemporary sacred music has been measured, and 'Alina' is arguably his most loved and imitated piece of work. 

Für Alina was first performed in Tallinn in 1976, and has become one of Pärt’s most-loved and widely appreciated works - regarded by many as an early, defining example of his signature tintinnabuli style. In the years since its release, Pärt has become the most performed living composer in the world, his approach to religious music seeping deep into our cultural landscape, from the avant garde to the mainstream.

Rendered with nothing more than piano and violin, this definitive ECM version from 1999 features Vladimir Spivakov, Sergej Bezrodny, Dietmar Schwalke and Alexander Malter providing alternate versions, handpicked by Pärt himself from recordings that were originally several hours long. It’s a masterclass in simplicity; an almost painfully beautiful rendering of emotional landscapes that, in the wrong hands, could have (and has, on many occasions, by so many) turned to schmaltz.

4AD re-master and press Pixies' 'Complete B Sides' compilation to vinyl for the first time with a full side of bonus live recordings - 25 years after its first release.

"Continuing the band’s 40th anniversary celebrations, Complete B-Sides: 1988-97 by Pixies is being reissued 25 years after its initial release, out June 26, 2026. Having been remastered, the compilation of the band’s timeless “other” tracks will be available on double black vinyl, double clear vinyl, and double CD; also marking the first time the release has been officially pressed on vinyl.

Originally released on CD in 2001, while the band were almost a decade into a hiatus, Complete B-Sides contained 19 b-sides from the band’s classic 4AD era (1988-1991) and featured beloved Pixies tracks including “Wave of Mutilation (UK Surf)”, “Into The White”, “Bailey’s Walk”, and “The Thing”. As Pitchfork said in their glowing 9.6 review, “If nothing else, this release proves that, like Dylan in the 60s and Brian Eno in the 70s, the Pixies were the blinding visionaries of the 80s. Virtually everything they touched was groundbreaking and revelatory, leaving one to wish they could only have touched more.”

For Complete B-Sides: 1988-97, all the tracks have been remastered from their original analogue tapes by Kevin Vanbergen - sounding amazingly fresh, it completes his extensive remastering work across the band’s catalogue. With the original tracklisting neatly fitting across 3 sides of vinyl, a fourth side of bonus live tracks has also been added, featuring six tracks culled from latter Pixies single releases including 1997’s Debaser re-release.

This new edition works as a companion piece to the band’s recent Live at the BBC compilation reissue, where designer Chris Bigg (v23) has created striking new art, taking photos from Simon Larbalestier’s archive that were originally slated for use by Pixies, but were later shelved. Both long-term collaborators with the band, they worked on both reissues in tandem to remember and honour the band’s late-visual director, Vaughan Oliver."

The ingredients were there, sure: Spacemen 3's druggy, phased feedback; Kevin Shields' master-tape warping sonic maximalism; Glenn Branca's symphonic, detuned repetitions; Robin Guthrie's chorus-drenched strums; and Brian Eno's heady long-form muzak. But nobody had spotted the connections before - it took a duo far removed from the inward-looking Thames Valley scene to unhook shoegaze's textures from its song structures. So, a year before Dave Pierce masterminded "rural psychedelia" on 'Flying Saucer Attack', multi instrumentalist and producer Scott Cortez and vocalist Melissa Arpin-Duimstra released 'Bloweyelashwish', a noisy collage of blown-out tape loops, brickwall distortions and angelic chorals that'd be remixed and repackaged for a Projekt Records reissue in 1994. 

This latest reissue from Numero has been remastered and bulked out with five additional archival discoveries, bundled with lyrics and a postcard for good measure. And although loveliescrushing would perfect the formula on 1996's heartbreaking 'Xuvetyn' before going on hiatus, their debut has aged like wine, its Portastudio grit reminding us exactly what's missing from the barrage of horizontal, faintly nostalgic ambient-noise albums released each Friday. Cortez and Arpin-Duimstra were genuinely peering into the future with this one. Think of it as a concrète precursor to Fennesz's laptop-damaged 2001 classic 'Endless Summer'.

São Paulo-born, Brighton-based Lau Ro taps into their roots on their second album, writing a series of raw, improvised, 4-track experiments that they expand into lush, tropicalia-inspired chamber pop.

In 2024, just after they released their debut solo album 'Cabana', Ro developed Flat Back Syndrome, a condition that meant that they couldn't stand or sleep easily. On medication for over a year, they got through trauma by relying on their favorite music: bossa nova, tropicalia and Música popular brasileira. And it's these elements that ended up inspiring 'Lau', an album that materialized in their mom's garage, improvised initially on a 4-track cassette recorder and later expanded in the studio, threaded with string arrangements from Finn Rees that contextualize Ro's drum parts, guitars, vocals and keyboards.

It's music that's best described as soft psychedelia, led by Ro's disarmingly beautiful voice that sings in Portuguese and English guiding us through knotty ambient pop constructions that sound effortlessly complex and never less than charming.

The drumfunk master displays sheer braindance finesse on a full debut for Planet Mu - spiritual cousin of his OG patrons, Rephlex - typically exploring rudely unbalanced meters on super crafty cuts for adventurous DJs and ravers. RIYL Plug, Paradox, AFX, Mike Paradinas, V Snares.

“dgoHn (pronounced “John") is the moniker of John Cunnane, who hails from somewhere between London and Essex. ‘Tessares,’ his fourth album but his first for Planet Mu, is playful, unconventional drum & bass that contrasts sparse effects and melodic elements with complex drumfunk and breakcore. He often uses unusual time signatures and head-spinning polyrhythms inspired by jazz and math rock, sometimes within the same track. Somehow he makes it sound effortless, and occasionally pretty as well, keeping a fine balance that never feels punishing; exploratory without getting lost.

He's built a name for himself over the last two decades performing live at festivals and events around the world, while collaborating with fellow artists such as Macc, Nic TVG, Jodey Kendrick and Badun as well as solo releases.

The album opens with ‘Waiting For’ which combines complex breaks with melodic fills, spacey effects and dubbed out vocals that feel like snatches of lost conversations - a combination he uses throughout the album giving it an eerie touch of humanity. Lead single ‘I Couldn't Remember So I Made Something Up’ is in 15/8 time. It feels like a conventional melodic drum & bass track, but the time signature disrupts the listeners’ expectations, while the detuned melody eases its sense of dislocation. ’Whistling On A Tuesday’ opens with a light echoey piano countdown into bass stabs which introduce heavy whirling amen breakbeats that switch between 180 and 120 bpm. ’Holly Can Swim But She Doesn’t Really Like It’ is the most rhythmically challenging track here. It feels hard to hang on to as its knotty breaks play out over bell chimes, like something Autechre might make if jungle was in their DNA. The album ends on the dubbed-out drumfunk of ‘7 Years Or More,’ with an arrangement that builds a filmic, dusty atmosphere of chimes and electric guitar, layering in vocals, vinyl crackle and echoing synth giving way to tough drums, before all that is taken away so that just a voice remains.”

DJ Plead drops a dead strong, fully romantic second album with ‘Please’ for Oslo’s Smalltown Supersound, pursuing his 2020 debut ‘Relentless Trills’ with a properly sticky balance of dancehall swivel and spatio-textural tactility - a perfect high-summer breeze tipped FFO DJ Python, Lenky, Taymour, Muslimgauze, Art of Noise...

For over a decade, Jarred Beeler aka DJ Plead has drawn on his Lebanese heritage in a unique catalogue of productions splicing microtonal flutes and keys wth dancehall and techno rhythms for the likes of Livity Sound, AD 93, and Air Max 97’s Decisions. With ‘Please’ he picks up where his debut album ‘Relentless Trills’ left off in 2020 for our ‘Documenting Sound’ series, taking the long form canvas as an ideal place for him to ease off the club gas and open out ideas with a heightened sensuality and romantic pathos which works a treat on swaying bodies as much as rested minds. 

Four years since that last solo shot, the ‘Quick EP’ for Livity Sound in ’22, and a plethora of collabs with TSVI, DJ Python, rRoxymore a.o., Plead emerges amid fellow auteurs - Actress, Barker, Jamal Moss - on Oslo’s long-running Smalltown Supersound with increased confidence in his own sound. It’s palpable in his sparing strokes of melody and unhurried pacing, coupled with a tender feel for weightless structures that are just as happy to shrug off the beats and get lost in their own thoughts as he gently grips the hips for an eyes-down shuffle.

The mah-ragga-nat single ‘Ride TV’ is a perfect example of his rudely atmospheric tekkerz, and about as hard as it gets, whilst elsewhere he really gives it up in lushest, hair-kissing style. His feel for richly humid, evocative ambience colours it front to back, from the seductive licks of ‘Return to Deuce’ thru the flamenco trills of ‘Traffic’, taking it to cinematic levels on the floating pads of ‘Seven Eight, Too Late’ and the Vangelisian plumes of ‘Open Era’, to an aerial cat’s cradle of flutes and subs to ‘Sush’ and hand-played drums of ‘Right-on Time.’

Sound of the summer!

New from Escho - 'Pusher' OST composer Peter Schneidermann (aka Peter Peter) taps his mates Majke Voss and Ice Age's Elias Rønnenfelt for his proper Bleeder debut, covering Lydia Lunch's 'Boy/Girl' and Fifty Foot Hose's 'If Not This Time' in the process.

Schneidermann is a familiar face on the Copenhagen scene, working closely with Nicolas Winding Refn on the 'Valhalla Rising' score as well as the scores for each of the 'Pusher' films. And he's been a member of the Escho family for years, so it was surely only a matter of time until he collaborated with Rønnenfelt. The band rush for the '90s on 'Marble Station', layering wall-of-sound guitars with deadpan vocals, while on 'Here Comes the Dead', they sound more like Black Country heroes Slade. The band's version of 'Boy/Girl' is stronger, led by rattling hi-hats and sleazy, Suicide-style guitars and they show off their range with their surprisingly tender version of 'If Not This Time'. It's all a bit knowing, sure, but it's Copenhagen, innit.

Música para Plátanos takes its name — and much of its inspiration — from the group’s recording studio, situated in the heart of a banana plantation on the humid north shore of Tenerife, Canary Islands.

"The ever-present sight of the green, sun-drenched fields surrounding their weekly sessions seeped directly into the music: improvised jams that are playful, layered, and deeply connected to place.

This release gathers a distilled selection from those sessions — a kind of “greatest rotten hits” distinct from their ongoing Imaginary Island Music volumes.

The album functions as a living archive bringing together a distilled selection of recordings spanning more than five years: from dusty, long-forgotten sessions to evolving tunes that have become staples of the band's live sets but have never before been committed to record. These long-form sessions served as a petri dish for the Lagoss sound, allowing their experiments to putrefy into their chaotic signature strain of cyber-exotica, unstable kosmische or heavily-corroded dub.

The title obvs nods to Brian Eno’s Music for Airports, but the logic is inverted. Instead of clean, ambient drift, the record inhabits a dense and fertile environment: polyrhythmic structures, Latin-infused electronics, and shifting counter-tempos that feel weighted by the local humidity.

Ultimately, Música para Plátanos is as much about the process as it is the place. Like the plantation outside, the music is subject to the elements; the tracks change shape depending on the heat of the day, what we drank, what we ate. It’s an unstable, honest harvest of sound—shaped by the weather and the state(s) of mind alike."

A six-part song cycle, Aliya Ultan's first solo album for Kou Records a celebration of the cello that stretches its range, letting it inhabit multiple registers at once.

Ultan came up with 'Looks Far Woman' when she felt burned out, expended utterly after years of arduous touring, teaching and constantly collaborating. But she still couldn't rest; her sessions became a way for Ultan to reconnect with the cello, using the hypnagogic state she was in to isolate its wooziest, most unusual textures. And its six songs examine each way the cello can be approached: on 'Road Song', it represents an open landscape as Ultan strums the strings and plays elongated drones; 'Wind Song' is gusty and dissonant; 'Mountain Song' is imposing and seismic; on 'Sky Song', Ultan lets weightlessness elevate her fictile notes; she reduces the sound to dusty granules on 'Seed Song'; and lets romance crack through the darkness on the moody finale, 'Heart Song'.

Pure charver archaeology: 1 hour of Mackem Makina importer, DJ Scott marshalling the Rockport and Air Max stompers at Hangar 13 v Uprising, May 2004. Fucking well aye mush!!!

As the story goes, DJ Scott was the first to bring the bouncy sound of Valencia queer megaclubs to England’s ultra macho working class North East, where, after a while, and the addition of MCs, it took root as local phenomenon; effectively a form of contemporary folk dance that mostly exists on the A19 leyline which joins Doncaster to Sunderland’s New Monkey club, but spiritually extends to Scotland, with an A66 spur to Redcar’s Powerhouse.

Long looked down on by snobs, the key working class sound of the NE has been rehabilitated and reclaimed in recent years to varying levels of ironic distance by London LARPers and expressly queer kids who would not have had a great time in the OG clubs in the early ‘00s, but can now enjoy the sound in their own spaces without fear of getting casually glassed or flegged-on. This tape looks back to that era when Makina, or Monta Musica, as it became known, was most often played at underage clubs - The New Monkey, or Hangar 13 - which only sold water and pop at the bar, but everyone was clearly tanning loads of wizz and pills. Depending on one’s proximity to Makina’s NE and Scottish stomping grounds, it’ll be either heaven or hell, but either way it’s 100% radge.

"Searching was self-recorded in Ronald’s living room on a 4-Track Tape Recorder in 1984. The recordings symbolise his engagement to cross-over everything that was known to him musically at that time. Most importantly, all recordings reflect his personal way of searching; searching for his own characteristic sound. Rhythmical patterns meet well balanced distortion, shaping the music into a mirror of his character. He was part of several Dutch Latin and Jazz bands, including Cascada and Ritmo Natural. With the latter he performed at Holland’s North Sea Jazz Festival. At this point Ronald is 78 years old, playing music every day.

Instruments: Acoustic Piano, Fender Rhodes Piano, Farfisa Organ, String Ensemble, Tenor Sax, Alt Sax, Soprano Sax, Clarinet, Alt Clarinet, Organ Bass, Micro Moog, Drums, Longa & Voices.”

As O.G. Jigg, Will “Memotone” Yates adapts his broad palette to the 16mm documentary and folk horror short imagery of Graham Vasey’s film project, The Black Tor, with an unmistakably vintage tone FFO Oskar Sala, Delia Derbyshire, Gruppo.

Named for the granite outcrop of Dartmoor, not too far from the musician’s native Bristol, ‘Black Tor Tracks’ depicts Yates in actual soundtrack mode, as opposed to imaginary. It gathers six instrumental accompaniments written between 2022-2026 that match the oneiric anachronisms of County Durham based Graham Vasey’s films with masterful blends of analog electronics and acoustic kit rendered in widescreen and dusted with a tone that reflects the filmmaker’s use of a 1950s Bolex and a 1930s Ensign Auto-Kinecam. 

If we weren’t informed otherwise, the music could easily pass for ‘50s or ’60 orchestral scores in a classic vein of British folk horror, or even Bernard Herrmann’s work for Hitchcock psychological thrillers - and by extension, even Oskar Sala in its electronic nuance - such is the timeless quality of Yates’ touch as O.G. Jigg. Severed from intended imagery the music remains potently synaesthetic, from the gloomy brood of ‘The Black Tor’, thru the celluloid dream sequence evocation of ‘The Sunken Kirk’, fine-wrought early electronic timbres of ‘Woodwose’ and ‘The Stones of Obb’, and hallucinatory tension of ‘Plough Stots’.

Good stuff.

Prolific Canadians Priori & Project Pablo, aka Jump Source, refract fine strains of deep house, indie-pop, dub and techno-pop on an expansive LP ft. guest vox by billy woods, CFCF & Loukeman and advised to admirers of Luomo, Nick Léon, Rosa Terenzi & D. Tiffany, Galcher Lustwerk.

Building on a decade of Jump Source 12”s for Pacific Rhythm and their self-titled label, Francis Latreille & Patrick Holland skip to the former’s mothership, NAFF, for the project’s variegated debut album. The range and subtle recombinant steez of ‘Fold’ plays deep into the duo’s role at the core of Canada’s renowned club sound, which has emerged over the past decade with canniest updates and refinements of ‘90s to ‘00s US, UK x EU house, techno, trance and beyond. All the above can be heard stripped for parts and reassembled according to classic club lust and galvanised with slick production sure to see it gather air miles.

Tune to tune they fine-tune nuanced aspects of style and pattern, from tweaked darkroom electro-house with over-the-shoulder vox in ‘Nice & Edgy’ calling to mind Cheap & Deep Productions, to the pearlescent ambient-pop of ‘Close’ ft. POiSON GiRL FRiEND. Standouts are registered in the deep house of ‘Empty Bars’ that finds cult rapper billy woods out of context on a groove co-produced with Nick Léon, and in the echoes of Canadian click-house pioneer Akufen on ‘Affect’ ft. Loukeman, thru the brisker deep techno-house of ‘Fade City’ ft. Deaton Chris Anthony, and the Luomo-esque, connoisseurs choice of ‘A Dull Knife’ faced by Harmony Index.

Writing for two double basses, vocals and electronics, Finnish-Australian composer Helen Svoboda dissolves her identity on 'Headwater', blending folk, improv and avant-garde sounds to create a personal reflection of her deep relationship with music.

Trained in contemporary jazz, experimental composition and improvisation, Svoboda is interested in how much she can actually say with the double bass itself, not just as an instrument but as a resonant body. With 'Headwater', she pushes against the modern concept of layering, trying instead to work with the materials she has at her fingertips: her voice and of course the double bass. And those two core sounds coarse through the album, providing it with the sonic and stylistic ballast it needs. Of course, traces of her jazz background are still perceptible, but Svoboda seems driven to create something new, reforming folk memories on tracks like 'Child' and 'Void of Space' and pushing the bass to its limits on 'Two Trees' and 'Morning Hepuli'.

Part 1 of a 12" series featuring Beatrice M.’s 'Sinking', the rudely aerodynamic debut LP where Tectonic's franco-british hope flexes a signature balance of ruff & smooth, building on a solid reputation earned via 12”s with her label, Bait, plus Tempa and Darwin’s SPE:C.​

Dubstep is not necessarily an album genre: beyond scant examples from the likes of Burial, Shackleton, or 2562, 12”s and DJ sets serve the sound in best context. However, Beatrice M.’s grasp of subtle sensuality and propulsive traction patently ends itself well to the format on ’Sinking’, with rolling, stepping and skanking permutations that deftly dance in the space between dubstep, proper, and its close-related cousins - UKG, broken beat, dub techno - with a finely measured proprioception of space, weight and pressure. 

Along with 2562’s recently dispensed ‘Lost Dubs 2006-09’, ’Sinking’ is arguably the best thing on Tectonic in recent memory, with a sound that revels in more ambiguous club suss. It’s the type of release primed for cans/buds as much as big cones, proving she’s equally adept at sublime tension, as in the languid ‘Ever’, as propelling a dance in the Martyn-esque wriggler ‘Motion’, and offbeat hood of ‘Disco Corner’.

items.body:
Before Freundliche Kreisel and Läuten der Seele, German producer and multi-instrumentalist Christian Schoppik teamed up with Katie Rich to found Brannten Schnüre, an experimental folk outfit that shuttled New Weird America into deepest, darkest Bavaria.

'Sommer Im Pfirsichhain' is Schoppik and Rich's second proper album, the follow-up to 2014's 'Aprilnacht' (that was re-issued on Aguirre in 2024) and the sunniest segment of their quadrilogy of records about the seasons. But don't expect anything particularly bright, like Schoppik's magickal later work, released on STROOM and Hands in the Dark, it's gear that owes its mood to Coil, the lower recesses of the Fonal catalog and Digitalis's fringe experimentation. Schoppik plays accordion, guitar and flute, but constructs most of the material from his archive of samples, a sound he would lean further into on those killer Läuten der Seele records. And Rich is left to murmur and sing over Schoppik's dense, often beatless compositions, songs that exist as textures and memories rather than definable elements. 

Just check 'Mithra Im Jardin Botanique', with its skewed organ vamps, downsampled loops and heaving, ritualistic vocals. Or 'Lichter Am Weiher', a faded rembetika memory that's filtered through a smoke-stained Bavarian lens. At its best, 'Somme Im Pfirsichhain' sounds like a forgotten reel of music that Werner Herzog left in a chest in a forgotten basement in Munich, a collage of Florian Fricke's experiments and folk musics recorded in-situ during his travels. Schoppik and Rich would refine their approach on their Freundliche Kreisel album for STROOM in 2022, but the four Brannten Schnüre albums are required listening for anyone interested in examining how Germany began to accept the concept of hauntology.

Unyielding motorik guitar juxtaposes worksite scrabble and chamber drone on two jams between the Harry Pussy guitarist and underground Swedish linchpins, Gustaffsson, Johannsson & Nordwall.

By cranks, for cranks: ‘Percussio / Economy & Discipline’ taps into a vein of refusenik energy that has fuelled both sides since the early ‘90s, with Bill Orcutt bringing his dare-to-differ guitar technique and tone to the concrète ritualism of iDEAL boss Joachim Nordwall in trio as Organ of Corti with Dan Johannsson (Sewer Election, Enhet för Fri Musik) and Mattias Gustafsson (Altar of Flies). Both sides of the equation have been stalwarts of the international avant-rock and noise networks for decades and continue to do their own thing without compromise here. 

A-side ‘Percusio’ is sharply defined by Bill Orcutt’s bloody-minded riff repetition, which appears to be sliced up on tape by Organ of Corti to near-psychotomimetic levels of intensity - like MES was in the studio imploring him, “nah, do it again, but fucking tighter!”. Side B, on the other hand, is all intrigue & stuff, luring into a workshop scene of icy keys keeping time while labourers shovel chuff knows what in the background.

Recorded between 1961 and 1963 and released on Impulse! Records in July 1963, Impressions documents John Coltrane’s classic quartet with pianist McCoy Tyner, bassist Jimmy Garrison, and drummer Elvin Jones.

"Two selections — “India” and “Impressions” originate from the group’s November 1961 engagement at the Village Vanguard, where the quartet was joined by Eric Dolphy on alto saxophone, bass clarinet, and flute and second bassist Reggie Workman.

These are paired with the studio recordings “Up ’Gainst the Wall” (recorded September 18, 1962) and “After the Rain” (recorded April 29, 1963 at Van Gelder Studio in Englewood Cliffs, NJ), the latter featuring Roy Haynes on drums.

Issued during the same period as albums including Coltrane and Live at Birdland, Impressions forms part of Coltrane’s early-1960s Impulse! discography, demonstrating the quartet’s unique power in both expanded live performance and studio contexts.

Verve’s Acoustic Sounds Series features transfers from analog tapes and remastered 180-gram vinyl in deluxe gatefold packaging."

Ricardo Villalobos runs rings around two trax from goat (JP)’s 2025 dance score in three durational, tempo-sloped parts for Paris-based Latency. Japanese no wave asceticism meets haughty house trot and lizard-hipped slink - 35 mins of it!

Now brought together by Parisian electronic atelier Latency, Villalobos pursues his preceding reworks of Reza Mortazevi’s hand-played percussion with a supple loosening of goat (jp)’s crystalline pulses in three distinct variations, tweaking the original timbales of ‘Orin’ away from avant-dance roots into 9 mins of heavily infectious wiggle swarmed with class, over-the-shoulder vocals, kinda something from his ‘Sei Es Drum’ series. ‘Factory’ on the other hand is taken for a longer ride in contrasting parts, recalibrating its cogs with a grittier swivel and unravelled loops of the OG in Variation 1, then slowing it all to a superb 110BPM version bound for the *special* folder and loosey goosey ends of the day/night.

MIKE's 10K imprint continues the trans-Atlantic conversation with the latest solo album from UK rapper Jadasea, featuring guest appearances from John Glacier, duentita, Anysia Kym and MIKE.

Following an acclaimed run of collaborations with MIKE (on 2024'a 'Old Earth' EP), Anysia Kim (on 2023's 'Pressure Sensitive') and Brooklyn-based producer Laron (on 'The Corner: Vol. 1'), Jadasea hones in on a suitably brittle sound on 'Holly Grove', rapping over a sequence of shortform instrumentals led by detuned synths and paper-thin trap beats. It's engaging gear, but comes into its own when Jadasea provides room for his guests: the throwback 'Intrinsick' is uses Kym's chorus perfectly, while John Glacier wakes up 'Lemon Cherry' with her deadpan reflections. On 'Entrance', duendita hands Jadasea the hook he's been missing, and on 'Collateral' MIKE's charisma gives the album a much-needed shot of adrenaline.

Echospace Detroit’s Stephen Hitchell is at his most romantic, club-friendly and elemental on these effortless dub house glyders, newly remastered by Pole for posterity and optimal immersion

Originally issued on 12” in 2015 and hard-to-find ever since, ‘Lost Sequence’ is classic, archetypal Echospace tackle. The OG goes for 14 mins of strutting deep house groove swaddled in velvet-coated textures dubbed to the rafters and happy to hold its lane for the duration, adding extra layers of conga and crackling atmosphere as it proceeds. Hitchell’s Intrusion dub pitches the same elements in a spring weather system, drenching everything in fine mist of elemental FX and loosening the bass drum to a satisfyingly soggy slosh for 16 minutes of hypnotic bliss out.
